method: Read every assigned body in full from family.packet.json before consulting initial_survey.json, recording all retained body paragraphs. Compared the family texts with the survey and cross-group source packet; quotations were checked as exact substrings of the cited packet paragraph.

outgoing_reviews.summary: Initiates a Herbert exchange from Osmaston/Derby context: asks for specifically located beetles, reports collecting and the Foxes' music meeting, and requests a long account of Herbert's proceedings. The promise to write and requests for a future account do not identify an earlier Herbert letter.

Explicitly answers a Herbert letter received only a few days earlier after a forwarding mistake, and says Butler supplied an account of the Welsh proceedings. It separately narrates two Whitley admonitions and Darwin's intervening humble answer; neither Whitley input is the Herbert letter.

proposed_links.reason: Exact incoming identity and receipt date remain unlocated.

evidence.quote: Very many thanks for your letter. owing to a mistake of not forwarding it, I only received a few days ago

proposed_links.reason: Two Whitley inputs and Darwin's intervening answer are separately narrated.

evidence.quote: When I arrived home, I received such a letter from old Whitley
merely received an acknowledgement of my extreme candour, another charge of the same description as before

outgoing_reviews.summary: A dated mock petition to the family for a £20 replacement double-barrelled gun, ending in a four-person subscription list. It is a self-contained request and supplies no incoming prompt.

Darwin writes on Susan's third sheet to Erasmus, apologizing for estrangement and reporting Cambridge rooms, prints, Fox, entomology, and friends. The packet explicitly identifies this as Darwin's contribution to Susan's sheet; no incoming Erasmus letter is named.

Initiates Caroline correspondence for Shropshire politics and gossip, while describing Cambridge, Henslow's lecture and geology help, Humboldt, Spanish, and tropical plans. The request for an answer is prospective.

Reports the expedition possibility through Wood, Henslow, Peacock, and partial knowledge of FitzRoy's letter, then asks Susan to inspect a held Henslow letter and locate books, bills, funds, and directions. The physical Henslow letter is held at home; its receipt and reading status are unresolved.

corrections.reason: The held Henslow letter remains a candidate source only; do not assert Darwin read it.

evidence.quote: Do not forward Henslows letter. you may open it, if you like

outgoing_reviews.summary: Reworks the previous day's family account after Wood received FitzRoy's discouraging letter and Darwin met FitzRoy. It gives detailed terms, ship arrangements, costs, and route, but the third-party FitzRoy-to-Wood letter remains oral/partial context.

corrections.reason: This supports revision/continuation of an earlier account, without proving posting or receipt.

evidence.quote: bringing up the other with me & altering it

proposed_links.reason: Chronology makes 115 the natural candidate; dispatch and receipt are unproved.

evidence.quote: bringing up the other with me & altering it

outgoing_reviews.summary: Adds equipment and medical commissions, describes FitzRoy's advice and the proposed route, and says the voyage is not settled. The phrase "since I received the letter" is too vague to identify a catalogued source; a request to write and receive an answer is future-facing.

A long same-day/update account covering a received parcel, Beaufort/FitzRoy arrangements, coronation observations, purchases, and route. The parcel is a nonletter receipt; "my letter written next day" likely points to 119 but is not uniquely identified.

proposed_links.reason: The relative reference likely points to 119 but is not uniquely identifying.

evidence.quote: you have received my letter written next day

proposed_links.reason: The object received is a parcel, not a letter.

evidence.quote: I have just received the parcel

outgoing_reviews.summary: Reports the three-day journey to Plymouth, the Beagle, FitzRoy, officers, delayed sailing, funds, and fluctuating confidence. References to former letters and money at the bank do not identify an incoming family text.

Updates Susan after cabins are assigned: Darwin now regards the voyage as fixed, explains his cabin and companion, arms, survey aims, and travel dates. It refers back to a Plymouth letter and announces a future Maer letter; neither creates a new incoming family target.

proposed_links.reason: The Plymouth reference fits 126, but the wording is not independently unique.

evidence.quote: you have received my letter from Plymouth

outgoing_reviews.summary: Answers a Caroline letter and separately acknowledges a Catherine letter, then discusses the tutor/furniture bill, living arrangements, and delayed sailing. It also says an unlocated letter to Susan was written the same day and recalls an earlier letter to Mr Ash. Date remains questioned as 31? October.

proposed_links.reason: The incoming Caroline letter is explicit, but its record and calendar date are unlocated.

evidence.quote: I received your letter the same day that I wrote to Susan

proposed_links.reason: A separate Catherine input follows the Caroline letter; no direct reply is stated.

evidence.quote: Since which I have had one from Katty

outgoing_reviews.summary: Updates Caroline on the tutor bill, Beagle fitting, social visits, sea-sickness, route, and correspondence logistics. The tutor-bill knowledge does not prove a new Caroline letter; "since Susan's date" establishes an earlier Susan-dated communication but not its identity or contents.

proposed_links.reason: This refers to Susan's dated communication and Darwin's own letter, but does not recover Susan's date or prove a direct response.

evidence.quote: I suppose you have received a letter from me since Susan’s date

proposed_links.reason: The bill could derive from prior knowledge or another channel; no new Caroline letter is explicitly acknowledged.

evidence.quote: The tutor’s bill is just as I expected

incoming_reviews.summary: Fanny apologizes for delaying a note, reports Brighton parties, asks for Shrewsbury scandal, and requests mysteries; it is social correspondence with no surviving Darwin reply identified in this family set.

Fanny explains that Cambridge and Mrs Burton's propriety fears delayed her reply, then discusses the Woodhouse travels, Bazaar, balls, and riding. No direct Darwin target survives in this family packet.

Sarah answers Darwin's Brighton effusion with a long social report: fancy ball, London visits, Forest gossip, family marriage rumors, horses, and an explicit request for his opinion. No surviving direct Darwin reply is assigned here.
Fanny apologizes for delayed response, reports parties, family visitors, riding, Cambridge, and asks when Darwin will come home. It supplies no surviving direct Darwin reply in this packet.

Sarah says Catherine dispatched a substantial letter addressed to Darwin and therefore delayed writing; she supplies Forest gossip, rumors, marriages, horses, and an invitation to continue. This explicitly attests Catherine's outgoing dispatch, but not Darwin's receipt or reading of it.

unlocated_references.description: Catherine dispatch addressed to Darwin; dispatch is attested, receipt and reading are not.

evidence.quote: very considerable dispatch composed by Catherine & directed to Mr. Charles Darwin

proposed_links.reason: Sarah reports witnessing the dispatch; this is not Darwin receipt evidence.

evidence.quote: witnessed the departure of a very considerable dispatch composed by Catherine & directed to Mr. Charles Darwin

incoming_reviews.summary: Fanny requests Darwin's account of Forest/Bliss/Darwin-Hall mysteries and discusses the sale, bachelors, and family gossip. No direct Darwin reply is assigned in this family set.

Fanny thanks Darwin for books and a swallow-tail, reports Oswestry theatre, family visits, painting, riding and billiards, and says she has forgotten the note's purpose. No direct reply is preserved here.

Fanny answers Darwin's request for a letter with Hunt-week, Forest, Clare's singing, beetle jokes, the Williams uncertainty, finances, and family news. No direct Darwin reply survives in this assignment.
Fanny writes at her father's request about his trip to London/Haleybury and Arthur's scrapes, and asks about Darwin's horses and partridges. No direct Darwin reply is identified.

Fanny sends Darwin a book through Francis, reports hunting and family activities, and promises another scrawl. Delivery of the book is a parcel/book channel rather than evidence of a letter prompt; no direct reply is assigned.
Fanny requests oil color, brushes, and a book to be brought from Whitney's, with a Monday visit and an order for Halston. This is a practical request; no direct Darwin reply survives here.

Charlotte congratulates Darwin after his fate is decided, discusses the delayed Henslow letter, FitzRoy, the added third year, family anxieties, and social plans. She says Elizabeth and she are going to the Bents at Derby for the music meeting next week and that a Welsh party heard intelligence about Darwin at Overton. These are social/contextual clues, not proof of a particular later Fox exchange.

proposed_links.reason: Event/topic overlap does not identify Charlotte's letter as the source of the Fox report or prove channel/timing.

evidence.quote: Elizabeth & I are going next week to the Bent’s at Derby for the music meeting

incoming_reviews.summary: Fanny sends a small purse as a keepsake and asks Darwin to remember Charles Mogg. No direct Darwin reply is assigned.

Fanny regrets missing Darwin before his departure, asks for his plans and a final farewell, and supplies extensive Devonshire, family, debt, horse, and cabin-related social commentary. She requests that the letter be burned; no reply is preserved in this family assignment.
Sarah encloses a promised hair pin, reflects on Darwin's departure and Woodhouse, promises a future account, and refers to a short reprieve/delay for his family. No direct Darwin reply is assigned.

Fanny says their letters crossed, quotes Darwin's concern about being forgotten, discusses the three-year absence and his sailing date, and asks for another letter if possible. The crossed Darwin letter is not among this family's outgoing records, and no further direct reply is present.

Fanny relies on Catherine's report that Darwin remained in suspense at Plymouth, then gives a long account of Sarah's wedding and asks for a final adieu. This is postdating every family outgoing target and should not be activated as a pre-target prompt.

findings.finding: Family/social incoming letters are evidence of possible correspondence context, not proof of Darwin's reading. Mostyn/Owen letters 37-44, 51, 77, 83, 85, 97, 134, 136, 137, 141 and 151 have no surviving direct Darwin target in this assignment; they remain incoming voices and must not be promoted merely because they were sent.

evidence.quote: I never was so horror struck as to receive your leetle note the other day
you told me you were going to Cambridge the end of the month
since I received your very agreeable effusion at Brighton
as Sarah wrote to you very soon after we came home
it was to tell you how very much oblig’d to you I was for the Books

I was very glad to receive your letter
Our letters must have crossed on the road— yours I received a few days ago

findings.finding: DCP-LETT-115's held Henslow letter is unresolved: P4 says Susan may open it, while P1 says Darwin heard only part of FitzRoy's letter through Wood. Candidate DCP-LETT-105 is therefore physical possession/possible reading context, not activated knowledge.

DCP-LETT-115 and 117 form a likely draft/revision or continuation sequence because 117 P1 says "bringing up the other with me & altering it"; neither text proves that 115 was mailed or received by Susan. DCP-LETT-122's "letter written next day" is likewise a candidate reference to 119, not a guaranteed identity.

DCP-LETT-145 contains two distinct incoming family inputs: Caroline's letter was received the same day Darwin wrote to Susan, then a Catherine letter arrived. The questioned date [31?] October and crossed/uncertain channels must remain explicit. DCP-LETT-146 confirms a Susan-dated communication but not a new Caroline letter.
DCP-LETT-133's Derby music-meeting plans do not identify the report in DCP-LETT-149 that Darwin heard of Fox at the Music Meeting; shared event vocabulary is insufficient for a knowledge link.

DCP-LETT-49 is the clearest family-group incoming relation: a Herbert letter was received late and answered. The two Whitley admonitions and Darwin's answer are separately narrated and remain unlocated rather than being collapsed into a surviving record.

limitations: The review establishes paragraph coverage and exact textual evidence only within the supplied packet and cross-group source packet; absence from the selected corpus is not proof that a letter never existed.
Incoming records do not by themselves establish physical receipt or reading by Darwin; where no outgoing acknowledgment exists, the review reports the text and leaves the target unlocated.
Date ranges, questioned dates, and composition-versus-dispatch distinctions are retained from the packet; no CSV sorting date was treated as an exact event date.
DCP-LETT-151 is postdated relative to all assigned outgoing targets and was kept as contextual incoming evidence only, with no pre-target activation.
